keep: The idea is named up front: measure along the eigenvectors, where each step only stretches each direction by its own eigenvalue, so n steps raise each eigenvalue to the power n.

The picture is the brief's Step it again: the F-flag stepped through A = [3 1; 0 2] with a counter n, a grid switch to the eigenvector grid where Dⁿ reads out, the pumps preset in a tanks view heading for 60 : 40 with the part above 600 L halving, and the shear preset with one line and the switch greyed out with its reason.

One worked example runs from the rule with numbers kept from lessons 2 and 5: (1, 1) has amounts (2, 1), three steps give (54, 8), which is (46, 8); P = [1 −1; 0 1], P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1]; A³ = PD³P⁻¹ = [27 19; 0 8], matching the square-grid multiplication; Aⁿ = [3ⁿ 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]. Practice works the tanks through PD³P⁻¹ = [0.65 0.525; 0.35 0.475] and the long run [0.6 0.6; 0.4 0.4].

The brief's misconceptions each get a screen: the power left off D (8, and a common mistake), enough eigenvalues but not enough eigenvectors (11, 12), independence confused (11's shear and 2I), D's order against P's columns (6), the forgotten λⁿ as λ × n (2, 4).

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13). Three footnotes, each on a rule he might look up, none naming a source. The capacitor pair is a new analogy from his trade with the same total and difference directions.
fix: Causal step skipped: 'One step multiplies the first amount by 3 and the second by 2, because each eigenvector is only stretched' leaves out why the mix splits. A matrix acts on a mix part by part (Matrices), so A(2 lots of (1, 0) + 1 lot of (−1, 1)) is 2 lots of A(1, 0) plus 1 lot of A(−1, 1). Say it.
False absolute in practice: 'Over many steps the eigenvalue biggest in size takes over' fails for a tie in size (1 and −1) or a start with none of that direction. Qualify it as the explanation does.
False absolute: '2I has 2 twice, and every arrow is one of its eigenvectors' includes the zero arrow, which lesson 5 ruled out. Say every nonzero arrow.
Overstated in practice: 'Whatever the start, the water ends up shared 60 : 40' says it arrives. It only heads there. Say it heads for a 60 : 40 share.
